learning_objective: 🎯 Put your skills to the test! Apply everything you've learned about grammar, structure, and proofreading in practical exercises to fix flawed texts.

main_concepts.simple_explanation: Often, words go missing when writing fast. A common editing exercise requires you to find the exact spot in a sentence where an article (a, an, the), preposition (in, on, at), or helping verb is missing and insert it.
This involves finding the wrong word and replacing it with the right one. It could be a wrong preposition ('good in math' should be 'good at math') or a wrong vocabulary word.

The golden rule of grammar: A singular subject takes a singular verb, and a plural subject takes a plural verb. Exercises frequently test tricky subjects like 'Everyone' (which is singular) or collective nouns.

Writers often accidentally jump through time. If a story starts in the past tense ('He walked to the store'), it cannot suddenly switch to the present tense ('and he buys an apple'). Editors must align all verbs to the correct timeline.
The ultimate test of an edited piece is how it sounds. If you stumble while reading a sentence aloud, it means the syntax is clunky and the sentence needs to be rewritten for better rhythm.

fun_activity.title: 🕵️‍♂️ The Error Hunt
fun_activity.instructions: Find a short news article online. Purposefully introduce 5 errors into it (change a tense, delete an 'a', swap 'their' for 'there'). Send it to a friend and time how long it takes them to act as the 'editor' and find all 5 mistakes!

exam_tips: 📌 In 'error-correction' passage questions, there is almost always exactly ONE error per line. Don't over-edit lines that are already correct.
📌 Pay special attention to prepositions (in, on, for, with) and articles (a, an, the). These are the most commonly tested errors in editing exercises.
📌 When fixing Subject-Verb agreement, ignore the 'filler' words between the subject and the verb. (e.g., 'The box of chocolates *is* empty', not *are* empty).
quick_recap: ⭐ Practice is the only way to build a subconscious 'radar' for spotting grammatical errors.
⭐ Always read the entire passage once for context before trying to fix individual line errors.
⭐ Tense shifting is the most common mistake student writers make; editors must be vigilant in enforcing time consistency.
